## What are we doing here?

This week's dataset is just the first million digits of $\pi$. Rather than doing anything mathematical with them, the fun question is: **does your birthday show up in $\pi$?**

Every birthday can be written as a 4-digit string (`MMDD`, e.g. `0324` for 24 March). Since $\pi$'s digits are believed to be [normal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_number) (every digit sequence appears about as often as you'd expect by chance), we'd expect essentially every possible 4-digit `MMDD` string to turn up somewhere in the first million digits - some more often than others just by luck.

So the plan is:

- Build a table of all 366 calendar dates (including 29 Feb) as `MMDD` strings.
- Slide a 4-digit window along the digits of $\pi$ and record every 4-digit sequence that appears, and where.
- Join the two on the `MMDD` string, so each calendar date picks up every position in $\pi$ where its birthday string occurs.
- Plot how many times each date's birthday shows up.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
pi_digits <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2026/2026-03-24/pi_digits.csv')
```

As a sanity check, let's confirm we can actually find a known chunk of $\pi$ (`3.14159`...`26535`...) in the data before completing the rest of our mission.
```{r}
pi_digits |>
  filter(digit == 0,
         lead(digit) == 1,
         lead(digit, n = 2) == 1,
         lead(digit, n = 3) == 1,
         lead(digit, n = 4) == 0,
         lead(digit, n = 5) == 3)
```
```{r}
temp <-  ymd("2000-01-01") + days(0:365)

```

## Building the birthday lookup

`temp` above gives us every date in a (leap) year. From there we turn each date into a zero-padded `MMDD` string (`bday`), and do the same for every 4-digit window of $\pi$'s digits (`vals4`), so the two can be joined directly.
```{r}
pi_digits |>
  filter(digit == 1, lead(digit) == 1, lead(digit, n = 2) == 2,
         lead(digit, n = 3) == 9, lead(digit, n = 4) == 7,
         lead(digit, n = 5) == 3)


library(lubridate)
library(latex2exp)
temp <- ymd("2000-01-01") + days(0:365)

head(data.frame(month = month(temp), day = day(temp)) |>
  mutate(month = ifelse(nchar(month) == 1, paste0("0", month), month),
         day = ifelse(nchar(day) == 1, paste0("0",day), day),
         bday = paste0(month, day)))


bdays <- data.frame(month = month(temp), day = day(temp), temp) |>
  mutate(month = ifelse(nchar(month) == 1, paste0("0", month), month),
         day = ifelse(nchar(day) == 1, paste0("0",day), day),
         bday = paste0(month, day))


pi_days <- pi_digits |>
  mutate(vals4 = paste0(digit, lead(digit, n = 1), lead(digit, n = 2),
                        lead(digit, n = 3)))

join_days <- bdays |>
  left_join(pi_days, by = c("bday" = "vals4"))

join_days |>
  group_by(bday) |>
  summarize(num_bday = n())


join_days |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_bar(aes(x = bday))
```

## How many birthdays actually show up?

Every one of the 366 possible dates turns out to occur somewhere in the first million digits of $\pi$ - some many more times than others. The bar chart above already hints at this, but a polar layout makes it easier to see how the counts spread across the calendar. Each wedge is a date, coloured by month, and its length is how many times that date's `MMDD` string appears in $\pi$.
```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 8.5
#| fig.showtext: true
library(showtext)
library(sysfonts)

font_add_google("Space Grotesk", "space_grotesk")
font_add_google("Fraunces", "fraunces")
showtext_auto()
showtext_opts(dpi = 300)

cream <- "#F8F5F0"
ink   <- "#222222"

month_cols <- colorRampPalette(
  c("#2F4F6F", "#4C7A5A", "#D4AF37", "#A8452F", "#6B2D3C", "#2F4F6F")
)(13)[1:12]

polar_plot <- join_days |>
  mutate(month_w = month(temp, label = TRUE)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_bar(aes(x = bday, fill = month_w), width = 0.75) +
  coord_polar() +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.8, 0))) + # empty hub for the pi
  scale_fill_manual(values = month_cols) +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = -Inf, label = "\u03c0", size = 40,
           family = "serif", fontface = "italic", colour = ink) +
  labs(
    fill = NULL,
    title = "Birthdays in Pi",
    subtitle = "How often each MMDD date appears in the first million digits"
  ) +
  theme_void(base_family = "space_grotesk") +
  theme(
    plot.background  = element_rect(fill = cream, colour = NA),
    plot.title       = element_text(family = "fraunces", face = "bold.italic", size = 24,
                                    colour = ink, hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle    = element_text(colour = "#9E7E38", size = 12, hjust = 0.5,
                                    margin = margin(t = 4, b = 6)),
    legend.position  = "bottom",
    legend.text      = element_text(colour = ink, size = 10),
    plot.margin      = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)
  ) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 1, keywidth = unit(0.4, "cm")))

polar_plot
```

```{r}
#| include: false
# thumbnail for the Data Lab listing (see `image:` in the front matter)
ggsave("media/tt12-polar.png", polar_plot, width = 8, height = 8.5, dpi = 150)
```

So yes - your birthday is (almost certainly) in $\pi$, and probably more than once!

* I'd like to disclose, the colours used in this plot were generated by Claude Code.


## About this Data

This week we're exploring the digits of $\pi$ with a [dataset submission](https://dslc-io.github.io/tidytuesdayR/articles/curating.html) in celebration of Pi Day (March 14).
The dataset contains the first one million digits of π, beginning with 3.14159...,
collected from publicly available sources and curated for analysis and visualization.

> "Pi is an irrational number, meaning its decimal representation never ends and never settles into a permanent repeating pattern."" — Eve Andersson, collector of the one million digits dataset

The digits are available from multiple open sources, including:

- [PiDay](https://piday.co/million/)  
- [Eneko Pi (one-million)](https://github.com/eneko/Pi/blob/master/one-million.txt)

These files provide the canonical sequence of π digits, starting with 3.14159, and have been tidied into a structured dataset for this week’s challenge.

This data comes from [Tidy Tuesday](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/blob/main/data/2026/2026-03-24/readme.md?plain=1).

## Data Dictionary

### `pi_digits.csv`

| variable       | class   | description                                      |
|:---------------|:--------|:-------------------------------------------------|
| digit_position | integer | The sequential index of each digit in the series |
| digit          | integer | The numeric value of the digit (0–9)             |
